backTranslations.41:
**Before the appointment**
- Add the appointment date in the Appointment tab. MenoMap shows how ready your notes are and what would make them more complete.
- Choose the topics and questions that matter most. Stick to three or four.
- Create your notes for the last 30 or 90 days. Check that your medication list is up to date.

**At the appointment**
- Hand over or show the first page. It was made to be read in under a minute: counts, averages, the heat calendar and your questions.
- Start with the question that matters most to you.
- If your health professional speaks another language, you can create the notes in that language.

**What the notes are, and what they are not**

They are a summary of what you logged, plus what you chose to bring from the Health app. They are not a diagnosis nor a complete medical record, and any pattern that appears in them is a coincidence check, not proof of cause. Your health professional may ask questions the notes cannot answer, and that is normal.

**After the appointment**

Add any new medication with its start date. In a few weeks, MenoMap can show your logs from before and after, which makes your next review easier.
backTranslations.42:
**Menopause** is a single point in time: the day that marks 12 months in a row without a period, when this is not explained by something else (such as pregnancy, some medications or surgery). In many countries it happens on average in the early 50s, but any age from the mid 40s to the mid 50s is common.

**Perimenopause** is the period of years leading up to that moment. Hormone levels rise and fall irregularly, so periods can become irregular, heavier, lighter, closer together or further apart. Many of the changes people associate with menopause, such as hot flashes, night sweats, sleep changes and mood changes, usually begin here, while periods are still happening. Perimenopause can last a few years or much longer, and is different for each person.

**Postmenopause** is everything that comes after the 12-month mark. Some symptoms calm down over time; others may continue for years.

Menopause can also happen earlier because of surgery that removes the ovaries, some cancer treatments or other health conditions. Menopause before age 40 is sometimes called premature ovarian insufficiency, and it is worth discussing with a health professional.

**How it is recognized.** For many people over 45, health professionals recognize perimenopause or menopause from their history and symptoms. Blood tests are not always necessary, because hormone levels fluctuate from one day to the next. They are more likely to be used when the person is younger or when the picture is unclear.

**What MenoMap does and does not do.** MenoMap cannot tell you which stage you are in. What it can do is keep an honest record of what you notice: flashes, sleep, mood and treatment, so that you and your health professional can look at the same picture.

backTranslations.162:
Health professionals call hot flashes and night sweats **vasomotor symptoms**. A hot flash is a sudden wave of heat, often in the face, neck and chest, sometimes with redness, sweating, a racing heart or a chill afterwards. A night sweat is the same thing during sleep, and can be strong enough to wake you or soak the sheets.

They are among the most common changes around menopause. Some people have few and mild ones; others have many a day, which disrupt work and sleep. For some, they lessen within a few years; for others, they last much longer.

**What can make them more likely.** People often notice patterns with alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, hot environments, stress or heavy bedding. This varies a lot from person to person, which is why tracking your own tags can be more useful than a general list.

**There are other causes.** Flushing and sweating can also come from thyroid problems, infections, some medications, anxiety and other conditions. If your symptoms do not follow the usual pattern, or come with weight loss, fever or feeling unwell, talk about it with a health professional.

**How to describe them well.** Useful details for an appointment:
- How many per day and per night, roughly
- How intense they are and how long they last
- What they interrupt: sleep, work, conversations, exercise
- What seems to happen before them
- What you have already tried, and whether it changed anything

MenoMap's Flash button and the later logging exist to capture exactly this without much effort.

**Help exists.** There are hormonal and non-hormonal treatment options, as well as practical approaches. Which ones suit you is a conversation to have with a health professional.

backTranslations.291:
Hormone therapy (often called HRT or HT) replaces part of the estrogen that the body starts producing less of around menopause. The main guidelines describe it as an effective treatment for hot flashes and night sweats for many people, and it can also help with other symptoms.

**It comes in different forms:** patches, gels, sprays, tablets and low-dose vaginal products for local symptoms, such as dryness. People who still have a uterus are generally prescribed a progestogen along with the estrogen, to protect the lining of the uterus.

**The benefits and risks depend on each person:** age, how long since periods stopped, personal and family history (for example of breast cancer, blood clots, stroke or heart disease) and the type and route of treatment. So it is a decision to make with a health professional who knows your history, not something an app can decide.

**Questions people often ask:**
- Is hormone therapy an option for me, and why or why not?
- What type and what form do you suggest, and why?
- What benefits can I expect, and how soon?
- What are my personal risks, and how do they compare with not treating?
- What should I watch for, and when should we reassess?

**If you already use it,** log it in MenoMap (You → Medications). MenoMap will show your flashes before and after you started, as a coincidence check and not as proof, so that you have something concrete to discuss at the reassessment.

MenoMap never suggests starting, stopping or changing a medication.

backTranslations.293:
Hormone therapy is not suitable for everyone, and some people simply prefer other paths. There are several.

**Prescription options.** Some non-hormonal medications have evidence that they reduce hot flashes. Among them are certain medications originally developed for other conditions and a newer class created specifically for hot flashes. Each has its own benefits, side effects and interactions, so a health professional can help you weigh them.

**Talk therapies and mind-body approaches.** Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) adapted for menopause has evidence that it makes hot flashes and night sweats less bothersome and improves sleep. Clinical hypnosis has also been studied.

**Practical changes people find helpful:**
- Layered clothing that can be taken off quickly
- A fan on the work desk and beside the bed
- A cooler bedroom and bedding that lets the skin breathe
- Noticing and easing your personal triggers (MenoMap's tags and experiments help with that)
- Regular physical activity and a stable sleep routine

**Supplements and herbal products.** The evidence is mixed or limited for many of them, quality varies and some interact with other medications. Tell your health professional or pharmacist everything you take, including products sold without a prescription.

**Try one change at a time.** MenoMap's two-week experiments compare your own logs before and during a change, which is easier to assess than an impression.

backTranslations.416:
Most appointments are short, and it is hard to remember a month of nights on the spot. People tend to remember the most recent days or the worst ones. A simple log fills that gap.

**What a diary gives your health professional:**
- How often the symptoms happen and how intense they are, not just that they happen
- Whether things are getting better, worse or staying the same
- What was going on around them: sleep, alcohol, stress, medications
- A starting point for comparison, if you try a treatment

**Keep it light.** A diary only helps if you keep it up. MenoMap was built around a one-tap Flash button and an evening check-in with four questions, so it takes seconds, not a whole notebook.

**Two weeks is a good start.** Two to four weeks of logs usually show a clearer picture than a single bad week.

**Bring your questions too.** Write down what matters most to you: the symptom that bothers you most, what you want to try or avoid and anything that worries you. MenoMap's Appointment tab helps you choose questions and prints them along with your notes.

backTranslations.479:
After 12 months without menstruating, **any vaginal bleeding should be evaluated by a health professional**, even if it happened only once, and even if it was just spotting or a light pink or brown discharge.

Most of the time, the cause turns out not to be serious. Thinning of the lining of the vagina or uterus is common, for example. But bleeding after menopause can sometimes be an early sign of a condition that is much easier to treat when found early. That is why public health guidance says to seek evaluation rather than wait.

**If you are on hormone therapy,** some bleeding patterns may be expected, depending on the type you use. Bleeding that is unexpected for your treatment, heavier than usual or outside the expected timing should also be evaluated.

**What to do:**
- Contact your health professional or health service and say you had bleeding after menopause.
- Note the date, the amount and anything else you noticed. MenoMap can keep this for you (You → Cycle).

MenoMap cannot tell why the bleeding happened. It will remind you to seek evaluation and will include this in your notes for the appointment.

backTranslations.529:
Sleeping badly is one of the most common complaints in midlife, and it rarely has just one cause.

**Night sweats** can wake you directly, or leave you too hot or too damp to fall back asleep.

**Other common factors:**
- Needing to urinate at night
- Anxiety or a racing mind
- Alcohol, which can help you fall asleep but often fragments the second half of the night
- Caffeine late in the day
- Pain, restless legs or the snoring of whoever sleeps with you
- Snoring or pauses in breathing, which can be a sign of sleep apnea (worth mentioning, especially if you feel very sleepy during the day)

**What usually helps.** A cool, dark room; bedding that lets the skin breathe and layers of clothing that are easy to take off; a fixed wake-up time; and less alcohol close to bedtime. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured, well-studied approach, and many health professionals can refer you to it.

**What to track.** For a week or two, note your sleep score, night flashes, alcohol and late caffeine. MenoMap's evening check-in and flash log do this in a few taps. If you use an Apple Watch, MenoMap can show your sleep and wrist temperature from the Health app alongside your night sweats, as context and not as explanation.

**When to seek evaluation.** Talk to a health professional if sleeping badly is affecting your safety (for example when driving), your mood or your daily life, or if you notice pauses in breathing or choking at night.

Every bleeding string and the bleeding article use 'após a menopausa' (after menopause, defined as 12 months without a period), avoiding the 'change years' trap; 'even once, even light' is preserved (130, 479); 'new, severe/intense, or with chest pain, shortness of breath or fainting, seek care now' is intact (278); emergency instructions (401, 717, 718, 388, 403), not-a-diagnosis, coincidence-check-not-proof, and never start/stop/change a medicine (400, 291) are all preserved with no added or weakened advice.
